passage_parts.label: Text A
passage_parts.text:
For years, theories regarding underlying connections between autism and intelligence have been proposed. The stereotype that autistic genius was freak mainly came from the 80’s classic movie Rain Man, which was a story inspired by a real autistic genius, Kim Peek. However, the association that autistic people are weird genius is not only deeply rooted in our minds but also originated from early period of time. In fact, some contemporary psychologists argued that talented scientists like Isaac Newton and Albert Einstein might have been autistic as well.
The 2022’s Netflix Top One show, a Korean series called Extraordinary Attorney Woo draws a lot of viewers’ attention to explore this connection. The series follows Woo Young-woo, a female rookie attorney with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) employed by a big law firm in Seoul. Being different from her colleagues, Woo’s communication way is regarded as odd, awkward, and blunt. While she faces prejudicial treatment at work and in her daily life, she effortlessly solves cases by focusing on details and legal regulations that nobody else spots. By solving each legal case through her superb intelligence and photographic memory, which is viewed as savant syndrome, she becomes an increasingly competent attorney. Savant syndrome is a rare and hyper-specific point on the autism spectrum. People with savant syndrome have exceptional abilities that is far beyond ordinary people. Experts estimate that savant-like tendencies present in 2-10% of the autistic population. The way Woo is characterized as a genius savant and aid common lawyers to solve difficult cases not only makes this series popular with audiences but also tells us what power media, like Netflix, can have for autism.
The stories we see from this drama reflect the full diversity of the autism spectrum. Gradually common people understand what life is like for autistic people and the challenges they face, as well as the huge contributions autistic people make to our society. For example, people can celebrate the show’s alleged intent to bring better awareness to autism in a country, South Korea, which intensely stigmatizes it. With an average nationwide viewership of around 17%, this drama is putting autism in front of a lot of Korean people.

passage_parts.label: Text B
passage_parts.text:
Perhaps I am an optimist after conducting this research through the feedbacks on the Internet, but I do believe some people will watch Extraordinary Attorney Woo and begin to think differently about autism and disability. Additionally, every episode of it ends with an important takeaway, like LGBTQ rights, cultural heritage preservation or even school pressure, which somehow comforts modern people.
I’m happy for those who relate to the show. I think, on an individual basis, that’s important. But it’s just as vital to remember that this is but one of the many very narrow windows into autism in media, and that we’re not like this phenomenal shows that can make all of our weaknesses or problems lie there to be examined and finally be realized.

questions.stem: Which of the following people may have Savant Syndrome?

options.A: A teen who memorizes over 12,000 books.
options.B: A scholar who participates in numerous conferences.
options.C: A speaker who possesses good communication skills.
options.D: A student who practices playing cello diligently.

options.A: The drama Extraordinary Attorney Woo also explores other issues in our society, such as gender diversity.
options.B: In Extraordinary Attorney Woo, Attorney Woo shows her outstanding talent in memory and intellect.
options.C: It is estimated that one out of five autistic people has savant-like tendencies.
options.D: Extraordinary Attorney Woo gets a high viewership and acquaints its viewers with what autistic people are.
